questions.question: The Hornbill Festival, celebrated to showcase tribal culture, music, dance, and sports, is associated with which Indian state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Nagaland**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Hornbill Festival** is an annual cultural extravaganza celebrated in **Nagaland** from **December 1 to December 10**.
 
• The festival is organized by the **State Tourism** and **Art & Culture Departments** of the **Government of Nagaland** to encourage inter-tribal interaction and preserve the state’s heritage.
 
• It is held at the **Naga Heritage Village** in **Kisama**, which is approximately 12 kilometers from the capital city, **Kohima**.
 
• Popularly known as the **Festival of Festivals**, it showcases the traditional **folk dances**, music, **indigenous games**, and crafts of the **sixteen major tribes** of Nagaland.
 
• The festival is named after the **Great Indian Hornbill**, a bird that holds a significant place in the folklore, songs, and **tribal traditions** of the Naga people.
 
• The event coincides with **Nagaland Statehood Day**, which is observed on **December 1** to commemorate the formation of the state in **1963**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Assam**:

 
 
• Home to the **Bihu** festival, which consists of three distinct celebrations: **Rongali**, **Kongali**, and **Bhogali Bihu**.
 
• Famous for the **Ambubachi Mela** held at the **Kamakhya Temple**.
 
 
 
• **Manipur**:
 
 
• Celebrates the **Sangai Festival**, named after the state’s rare **brow-antlered deer** found in **Keibul Lamjao National Park**.
 
• Other notable festivals include **Yaoshang** and the **Kang** festival.
 
 
 
• **Meghalaya**:
 
 
• Known for the **Wangala Festival** (100 Drums Festival) celebrated by the **Garo tribe** to mark the end of the harvest season.
 
• The **Cherry Blossom Festival** in **Shillong** has also become a major international attraction.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about volcanism is most accurate in the context of geomorphic processes?

options.text: It is controlled by rainfall and temperature
It requires running water to operate
It mainly builds or elevates parts of the crust

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It mainly builds or elevates parts of the crust**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Volcanism** is a primary **endogenic geomorphic process** driven by the internal heat of the Earth, which results from **radioactive decay** and primordial heat from the core.
 
• Geomorphic processes are generally classified into two categories: **endogenic** (internal) and **exogenic** (external). While exogenic processes tend to reduce relief, endogenic processes like volcanism are **constructive** or aggradational in nature.
 
• The process involves the movement of molten rock or **magma** from the mantle toward the surface. When this magma cools and solidifies on the surface as **lava**, it forms new landmasses and geographic features.
 
• Common landforms created by volcanism include **volcanic mountains**, **cinder cones**, **composite volcanoes**, and vast **lava plateaus** such as the **Deccan Traps** in India or the **Columbia Plateau** in the USA.
 
• In the context of the Earth’s **crustal evolution**, volcanism is responsible for the continuous addition of material to the lithosphere, thereby **elevating** the terrain and creating structural relief.
 
• Hence, the statement that volcanism mainly builds or elevates parts of the crust is correct.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Exogenic Processes**:

 
 
• These processes, such as **weathering**, **erosion**, and **mass wasting**, are driven by external forces like **solar energy** and **gravity**.
 
• They are primarily **degradational**, meaning they work to wear down and lower the existing landforms to a base level.
 
• Factors like **rainfall**, **temperature fluctuations**, and **running water** are the primary agents of these external processes.
 
 
 
• **Diastrophism**:
 
 
• This is another endogenic process that includes **orogenic** (mountain-building) and **epeirogenic** (continent-building) forces.
 
• Like volcanism, **diastrophism** results in the deformation, uplifting, or subsidence of the Earth’s crust.
 
 
 
• **Magmatic Features**:
 
 
• **Intrusive landforms** (plutonic) are formed when magma cools within the crust (e.g., **batholiths**, **laccoliths**, **sills**, and **dykes**).
 
• **Extrusive landforms** are formed when magma reaches the surface as lava and solidifies.

questions.question: What is the main objective of India's fiscal policy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Economic growth and stability**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fiscal Policy** in India is the framework through which the **Ministry of Finance** manages government spending and taxation to influence the national economy.
 
• The foremost objective is **Economic Growth**, achieved by increasing the **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** through strategic investments in **Infrastructure**, **Agriculture**, and **Industrial sectors**.
 
• **Economic Stability** refers to the government's effort to maintain **Price Stability** and control **Inflation**, ensuring that the cost of living remains manageable for the general public.
 
• It serves as a tool for **Resource Mobilization**, where the government generates revenue through **Direct and Indirect Taxes** to fund essential public services and developmental projects.
 
• Another vital goal is **Full Employment**, where the government uses budgetary allocations to create job opportunities in both rural and urban areas to reduce poverty.
 
• The policy also aims at **Reducing Inequalities** by implementing **Progressive Taxation** and providing **Subsidies** to the underprivileged sections of society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Inflation and Fiscal Deficit**:

 
 
• **Inflation**: While **Monetary Policy** (managed by the **RBI**) is the primary tool for inflation control, fiscal policy supports it by managing **Public Expenditure**. Increasing inflation is a negative economic outcome, not an objective.
 
• **Fiscal Deficit**: This is the excess of total expenditure over total receipts (excluding borrowings). The **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003**, actually mandates the government to reduce the fiscal deficit to ensure long-term **Macroeconomic Stability**.
 
 
 
• **Foreign Trade**:
 
 
• India's fiscal measures, such as **Customs Duties** and **Export Incentives**, are designed to boost **Foreign Exchange Reserves** and promote exports rather than reducing overall trade.
 
 
 
• **Instruments of Fiscal Policy**:
 
 
• **Budgeting**: The annual financial statement presented under **Article 112** of the **Constitution of India**.
 
• **Taxation**: Includes **GST**, **Income Tax**, and **Corporate Tax**.
 
• **Public Debt**: Internal and external borrowings to fund developmental gaps.

questions.question: Harshavardhana’s sister, Rajyashri, was married to whom among the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Grahavarman**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Rajyashri** was the sister of the great north Indian emperor **Harshavardhana** and the daughter of **Prabhakaravardhana**, the first notable king of the **Pushyabhuti** (Vardhana) dynasty of **Thanesar**.
 
• She was married to **Grahavarman**, the last important ruler of the **Maukhari dynasty**, who ruled over **Kannauj** in the early **7th century AD**.
 
• The marriage was a critical **geopolitical alliance** designed to protect the borders of both kingdoms against the rising threats from the rulers of **Malwa** and **Gauda**.
 
• Shortly after the marriage, **Grahavarman** was attacked and killed by **Devgupta** (the king of Malwa) who acted in collaboration with **Shashanka** (the king of Bengal).
 
• Following **Grahavarman’s** assassination, **Rajyashri** was imprisoned in **Kannauj**, which triggered a series of military campaigns by her brothers, **Rajyavardhana** and later **Harshavardhana**, to avenge the family and rescue her.
 
• After being rescued from the **Vindhya forests** just as she was about to commit self-immolation, **Rajyashri** co-ruled **Kannauj** with **Harshavardhana**, leading to the unification of the **Thanesar** and **Kannauj** administrative seats.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rudrasena II**:

 
 
• He was a ruler of the **Vakataka dynasty** in the Deccan.
 
• He is historically significant for his marriage to **Prabhavatigupta**, the daughter of the **Gupta** emperor **Chandragupta II**, which established a strong **Gupta-Vakataka** alliance.
 
 
 
• **Shashanka**:
 
 
• He was the king of the **Gauda Kingdom** (modern-day Bengal) and is regarded as the first major independent king of **Bengal**.
 
• He was a staunch rival of **Harshavardhana** and was responsible for the treacherous murder of Harsha’s elder brother, **Rajyavardhana**.
 
 
 
• **Devgupta**:
 
 
• He was a ruler of the **Later Gupta** dynasty of **Malwa**.
 
• He played a central role in the conflict by killing **Grahavarman** and capturing **Rajyashri** before being defeated by **Rajyavardhana**.

questions.question: Which schedule contains the assigned functions of the Rural Local Self Government or the Panchayati Raj?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**11th Schedule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **11th Schedule** was added to the **Constitution of India** by the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**, which came into force on **April 24, 1993**.
 
• This schedule establishes the functional domain for **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)**, representing the system of **Rural Local Self-Government** in India.
 
• It specifies **29 functional items** over which Panchayats have the power and authority to prepare plans for **economic development** and **social justice**.
 
• The specific subjects included in the schedule range from **Agriculture** and **Land Improvement** to **Minor Irrigation**, **Social Forestry**, **Small Scale Industries**, **Rural Housing**, and **Drinking Water**.
 
• The legislative basis for this schedule is **Article 243-G**, which empowers State Legislatures to endow Panchayats with necessary powers to function as institutions of self-government.
 
• The implementation of this schedule was a realization of the **Gandhian principle** mentioned in **Article 40** of the **Directive Principles of State Policy**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **12th Schedule**:

 
 
• Inserted by the **74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**.
 
• It defines the powers, authority, and responsibilities of **Municipalities** (Urban Local Self-Government) and contains **18 functional subjects** under **Article 243-W**.
 
 
 
• **10th Schedule**:
 
 
• Added by the **52nd Amendment Act, 1985**, commonly known as the **Anti-Defection Law**.
 
• It contains provisions regarding the **disqualification** of members of **Parliament** and **State Legislatures** on the ground of defection to another political party.
 
 
 
• **9th Schedule**:
 
 
• Introduced by the **1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951** to protect **land reform** and other laws from **judicial review**.
 
• While it initially aimed to prevent legal challenges based on **Fundamental Rights**, the **Supreme Court** ruled in **2007 (IR Coelho case)** that laws added after 1973 are subject to the **Basic Structure Doctrine**.

questions.question: Articles 245 to 255 of Part XI of the Indian Constitution primarily deal with which aspect of Centre-State relations?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Legislative relations**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Part XI** of the **Indian Constitution** establishes the framework for the relationship between the **Union** and the **States**, which is a core feature of Indian federalism.
 
• **Chapter I** of Part XI, comprising **Articles 245 to 255**, specifically governs the **Legislative relations**, defining how law-making powers are distributed between the **Parliament** and **State Legislatures**.
 
• **Article 245** specifies the **territorial extent** of legislation, allowing Parliament to make laws for the entire country and State Legislatures for their respective territories.
 
• **Article 246** deals with the distribution of subject matter through the **Seventh Schedule**, which contains the **Union List**, **State List**, and **Concurrent List**.
 
• **Article 248** grants **residuary powers** to the **Parliament**, meaning it has exclusive authority to legislate on any matter not listed in the Concurrent or State Lists.
 
• **Article 249** empowers the Parliament to legislate on a **State List** subject if the **Rajya Sabha** declares it necessary in the **national interest** by a two-thirds majority.
 
• **Article 254** outlines the **Doctrine of Repugnancy**, stating that if a State law conflicts with a Central law on a **Concurrent List** subject, the Central law generally prevails.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Administrative relations**:

 
 
• These are detailed in **Chapter II** of **Part XI**, specifically from **Articles 256 to 263**.
 
• They focus on the **executive power** coordination, the role of **All India Services**, and the creation of an **Inter-State Council** under **Article 263**.
 
 
 
• **Financial relations**:
 
 
• These are governed by **Part XII** of the Constitution, encompassing **Articles 264 to 293**.
 
• Key aspects include the distribution of **tax revenues**, **Grants-in-aid**, and the mandatory appointment of the **Finance Commission** under **Article 280** every five years.
 
 
 
• **Judicial relations**:
 
 
• India does not have a dual judicial system; instead, it features a **single integrated judicial system**.
 
• The **Supreme Court** acts as the apex body, followed by **High Courts** and **Subordinate Courts**, ensuring uniformity in the application of both Central and State laws.

questions.question: The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) was enacted in 1999 to replace the earlier FERA law. In which year did FEMA officially come into force?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2000**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA)** was passed by the **Indian Parliament** in **1999** as a replacement for the older and more stringent **Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA)** of **1973**.
 
• Although the Act is titled **FEMA, 1999** and received the **Presidential assent** on **December 29, 1999**, it was officially notified and came into force across the country on **June 1, 2000**.
 
• The primary objective of **FEMA** is to consolidate and amend the law relating to **foreign exchange** with the aim of facilitating **external trade** and payments and for promoting the orderly development and maintenance of the **foreign exchange market** in India.
 
• Unlike its predecessor, **FEMA** shifted the focus from **regulation** (restriction) to **management**, aligning India's financial framework with the **liberalization** policies initiated in the **1990s**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA), 1973**:

 
 
• This was the predecessor to **FEMA** and was characterized by its **prohibitive nature**.
 
• Under **FERA**, any violation was considered a **criminal offense**, punishable with imprisonment, whereas under **FEMA**, violations are **civil offenses** punishable by **monetary penalties**.
 
 
 
• **Enforcement Directorate (ED)**:
 
 
• The **Directorate of Enforcement**, under the **Ministry of Finance**, is the primary agency responsible for investigating suspected contraventions of **FEMA** provisions.
 
• It has the power to adjudicate cases and impose penalties on individuals or corporate entities found in violation of the Act.
 
 
 
• **Role of RBI**:
 
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** plays a central role in administering **FEMA** by controlling **current account** and **capital account** transactions.
 
• The **RBI** issues detailed **Master Directions** and circulars to regulate the flow of **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** and **External Commercial Borrowings (ECB)**.

questions.question: The Government of India Act, 1935, provided ______________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Provincial autonomy and federal structure**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1935** was a significant milestone that provided for the establishment of an **All-India Federation**. This federation was intended to consist of **British Indian Provinces** and **Princely States** as constituent units.
 
• The Act abolished the system of **Dyarchy** in the provinces, which had been introduced by the **1919 Act**, and replaced it with **Provincial Autonomy**. This granted provinces a separate legal identity and the freedom to operate as autonomous units of administration.
 
• It introduced **Responsible Government** in provinces, meaning the **Governor** was required to act on the advice of ministers who were accountable to the **Provincial Legislature**.
 
• The Act distributed legislative powers between the **Centre** and the **Provinces** through three lists: the **Federal List** (59 items), the **Provincial List** (54 items), and the **Concurrent List** (36 items), while **Residuary Powers** were vested in the **Viceroy**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dyarchy in Provinces**:

 
 
• This system was a feature of the **Government of India Act, 1919** (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms). Under the **1935 Act**, Dyarchy was instead proposed at the **Central level**, though this part of the Act was never implemented.
 
 
 
• **Extension of Communal Representation**:
 
 
• While **Separate Electorates** were first introduced for Muslims in **1909**, the 1935 Act extended this principle to **Depressed Classes** (Scheduled Castes), **Women**, and **Labor** (Workers).
 
 
 
• **Institutional Establishments**:
 
 
• The Act led to the creation of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** in 1935 to regulate national currency and credit.
 
• It also provided for the setting up of a **Federal Court**, which was established in **1937**, and **Provincial Public Service Commissions**.

questions.question: Which shortcut saves the current file in Microsoft Word or Microsoft Excel?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ctrl + S**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **Microsoft Word** and **Microsoft Excel**, the keyboard shortcut **Ctrl + S** is the standard command used to **Save** the active document or workbook to the storage drive.
 
• If the file has already been saved, pressing **Ctrl + S** instantly updates the existing file with any **new modifications** made since the last save operation.
 
• For a **new document** that has not yet been assigned a name, this shortcut triggers the **Save As** interface, requiring the user to select a **file format** (such as .docx or .xlsx) and a **directory location**.
 
• The **Ctrl** (Control) key acts as a modifier, and the letter **S** serves as a mnemonic for **Save**, a convention maintained across nearly all **Windows-based applications** to ensure **data integrity** and prevent work loss.
 
• This command interacts with the **Office Fluent User Interface** to bypass the manual process of clicking **File** and then **Save** on the **Quick Access Toolbar**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ctrl + Tab**:

 
 
• Functionally used to **switch between open tabs** in web browsers or to move between different **child windows** within a single parent application window.
 
 
 
• **Ctrl + V**:
 
 
• The universal shortcut for the **Paste** command, which retrieves data from the **System Clipboard** and inserts it at the **insertion point** or selected cell.
 
 
 
• **Ctrl + F**:
 
 
• Activates the **Find** feature, opening a **Navigation Pane** or dialog box to search for specific **text strings**, **formatting**, or **special characters** within the file.
 
 
 
• **F12 Function Key**:
 
 
• While **Ctrl + S** performs a standard save, the **F12** key is specifically designed to open the **Save As** dialog box directly, even if the file has already been saved.

questions.question: India follows which model of citizenship under its Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**One: only Indian citizenship**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Constitution of India** establishes a system of **Single Citizenship**, meaning that despite India being a **Federal State** with a dual polity (Centre and States), there is only one citizenship for the entire country.
 
• This provision is detailed in **Part II** of the Constitution, encompassing **Articles 5 to 11**, which define who was eligible for citizenship at the time of the Constitution’s commencement on **January 26, 1950**.
 
• Unlike other federal systems, an Indian citizen owes allegiance only to the **Union of India** and does not possess a separate citizenship for the state in which they reside, such as **Kerala** or **Rajasthan**.
 
• The concept of single citizenship in India was inspired by the **British Constitution** (United Kingdom) to foster **national unity**, **fraternity**, and to prevent regionalism from undermining the integrity of the nation.
 
• All citizens of India, regardless of their place of birth or residence, enjoy uniform **Fundamental Rights** and political privileges across the whole of the **Indian Territory**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dual Citizenship Model**:

 
 
• In countries like the **United States of America (USA)** and **Switzerland**, a dual citizenship model is followed where an individual is a citizen of the **National Government** and also a citizen of a particular **State**.
 
• This can sometimes lead to different sets of rights or laws applicable to citizens depending on their state of residence, a situation the Indian framers avoided to ensure equality.
 
 
 
• **Citizenship Act, 1955**:
 
 
• While the Constitution provides the framework, the **Parliament** used its powers under **Article 11** to enact the **Citizenship Act, 1955**, which governs the **acquisition** and **loss** of citizenship after 1950.
 
• Indian citizenship can be acquired through five methods: **Birth**, **Descent**, **Registration**, **Naturalization**, and **Incorporation of Territory**.
 
 
 
• **Termination of Citizenship**:
 
 
• The Indian law is strict regarding single citizenship; if an Indian citizen voluntarily acquires the citizenship of another country, their **Indian citizenship** is automatically terminated under the principle of **Renunciation** or **Termination**.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Directive Principles of State Policy is correct?

options.text: They can be enforced by any citizen through writ petitions.
They are enforceable by the courts as Fundamental Rights.
They are non-justiciable guidelines that aim to establish a just society.
They are absolute and cannot be amended under any circumstance.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They are non-justiciable guidelines that aim to establish a just society.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** are enumerated in **Part IV** of the **Constitution of India**, covering **Articles 36 to 51**. These principles are intended to be the **fundamental goals** that the State must strive to achieve while formulating policies and enacting laws.
 
• **Article 37** of the Constitution explicitly declares that these principles are **not enforceable by any court**, which makes them **non-justiciable** in nature. This distinguishes them from **Fundamental Rights**, which can be legally enforced if violated. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The primary objective of the DPSP is to establish **social and economic democracy** and transform India into a **Welfare State**. They direct the State to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order permeated by **social, economic, and political justice**.
 
• Since the DPSP are non-justiciable, no citizen can approach the **Supreme Court** or **High Courts** through **writ petitions** (under **Article 32** or **Article 226**) to demand their implementation. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• Unlike **Fundamental Rights** (Part III), which are legally enforceable, the DPSP are moral obligations and political directives for the government. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The DPSP are not absolute and can be amended by the **Parliament of India**. Significant amendments include the **42nd Amendment Act of 1976** (which added **Articles 39A, 43A, and 48A**) and the **97th Amendment Act of 2011** (which added **Article 43B**). ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Origins and Classification:**

 
 
• **Source:** The concept of DPSP was borrowed from the **Irish Constitution** of 1937.
 
• **Socialistic Principles:** These aim at providing social and economic justice, such as **Article 39** (Equal pay for equal work) and **Article 41** (Right to work and education).
 
• **Gandhian Principles:** These represent the program of reconstruction enunciated by **Mahatma Gandhi**, including **Article 40** (Organization of village panchayats) and **Article 47** (Prohibition of intoxicating drinks).
 
• **Liberal-Intellectual Principles:** These reflect the ideology of liberalism, such as **Article 44** (Uniform Civil Code) and **Article 50** (Separation of judiciary from executive).
 
 
 
• **Critical Jurisprudence:** In the **Minerva Mills Case (1980)**, the **Supreme Court** held that the Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the **balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **speed of sound** in a gas is primarily determined by the **temperature** of the medium rather than its pressure or density alone.
 
• As the **temperature** of the air increases, the **kinetic energy** of the air molecules increases, causing them to move and vibrate more rapidly.
 
• Sound is a **mechanical wave** that travels through the **periodic collision** of particles; therefore, faster-moving molecules can transmit the **vibrational energy** of the sound wave more quickly through the air.
 
• Mathematically, the relationship is expressed as v = sqrt{(gamma RT)/(M)} , where **v** is the speed, **T** is the **absolute temperature**, **R** is the gas constant, **M** is the molar mass, and **gamma** is the **adiabatic index**.
 
• Because **v** is proportional to the **square root of T**, the speed of sound increases as the **temperature** rises.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Numerical Impact of Temperature**:

 
 
• At **0 degrees Celsius**, the speed of sound in dry air is approximately **331 meters per second**.
 
• At **20 degrees Celsius** (room temperature), the speed increases to approximately **343 meters per second**.
 
• For every **1 degree Celsius** rise in temperature, the speed of sound in air increases by roughly **0.6 meters per second**.
 
 
 
• **Effect of Medium Properties**:
 
 
• **Humidity**: Increased humidity also increases the speed of sound because **water vapor** is less dense than dry air, decreasing the overall **density** of the air mixture.
 
• **Density and Elasticity**: While speed is inversely proportional to the square root of **density**, in gases, the increase in **temperature** has a much more dominant effect on the **elastic properties** than the resulting decrease in density.

questions.question: Pressure is measured in which SI unit?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**N/m2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pressure** is defined as the physical magnitude of the **normal force** exerted per unit **surface area** over which that force is distributed.
 
• The mathematical relationship is expressed by the formula **P = F / A**, where **P** represents pressure, **F** denotes the perpendicular force, and **A** denotes the area of the surface.
 
• In the **International System of Units (SI)**, the standard unit of **force** is the **Newton (N)** and the standard unit of **area** is the **square meter (m²)**.
 
• By substituting these base units into the pressure formula, the derived SI unit is calculated as **Newton per square meter**, commonly written as **N/m²**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pascal (Pa)**:

 
 
• The unit **N/m²** is formally designated as the **Pascal (Pa)** in the SI system, named after the scientist **Blaise Pascal**.
 
• One Pascal is a relatively small amount of pressure; for instance, the **standard atmospheric pressure** at sea level is approximately **101,325 Pa**.
 
 
 
• **Analysis of Other Units**:
 
 
• **N/m**: This is the SI unit for **Surface Tension** and the **Spring Constant** (stiffness of a spring).
 
• **N·m**: This is the SI unit for **Torque** (moment of force) and is also equivalent to the **Joule (J)**, the unit for **Work** and **Energy**.
 
• **Dimensional Formula**: The dimensions of pressure are **[M¹ L−¹ T−²]**, derived from the dimensions of force divided by area.
 
 
 
• **Other Pressure Units**:
 
 
• **Bar**: Used in meteorology, where **1 bar = 10⁵ Pa**.
 
• **Torr**: Often used in vacuum physics, where **1 Torr ≈ 133.32 Pa**.

__
 
• The **Tertiary sector** comprises activities that do not produce a physical good by themselves but provide support or aid for the production process. This is why it is widely referred to as the **Service Sector**.
 
• **Trade** is a fundamental component of this sector as it involves the exchange of goods and services between producers and consumers, facilitating the flow of the **economy**.
 
• **Services** encompass a wide range of intangible benefits, including **transportation**, **communication**, **banking**, and **insurance**, all of which are essential for the smooth functioning of primary and secondary industries.
 
• Economic activities in this category help in the distribution of finished products from the factory to the market, making **wholesale** and **retail** trade vital tertiary functions.
 
• Unlike the primary and secondary sectors, the tertiary sector produces **services** rather than **tangible goods**, providing professional expertise and infrastructure to society.

• Commonly known as the **Agriculture and Allied Sector**.
 
• It involves the direct extraction and use of natural resources such as **farming**, **mining**, **fishing**, and **forestry**.
 
 
 
• **Secondary Sector**:
 
 
• Commonly known as the **Industrial Sector**.
 
• It covers activities where raw materials are transformed into finished products through **manufacturing**, **construction**, and **processing**.

• A specialized subset of the tertiary sector focusing on **knowledge-based** services.

questions.question: What is the primary reason for the rapid population growth in developing countries during the second stage of the Demographic Transition Model?

options.text: Low birth rates and high death rates
Low birth rates and low death rates
High birth rates and high death rates
High birth rates and declining death rates

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**High birth rates and declining death rates**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **second stage** of the **Demographic Transition Model (DTM)** is known as the **early expanding** phase, where a country transitions from an agrarian economy toward industrialization.
 
• During this stage, **birth rates** remain high because social and cultural traditions, such as the preference for large families and the need for labor in farming, change very slowly.
 
• The **death rate** begins to fall sharply due to improvements in **food security**, **basic hygiene**, and **public health** measures like access to clean water and mass vaccinations.
 
• The resulting gap between the **high fertility** and **rapidly falling mortality** creates a high rate of **natural increase**, leading to a sudden and rapid increase in the total population.
 
• Historically, many developing nations entered this stage during the **20th century** as they imported medical technology and agricultural techniques from more developed regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Stage 1: High Stationary**

 
 
• This stage is marked by **high birth rates** and **high death rates** due to famine, poor sanitation, and lack of medical knowledge, resulting in a stable but low total population.
 
 
 
• **Stage 3: Late Expanding**
 
 
• In this phase, **birth rates** start to decline as a result of urbanization, increased access to **contraception**, and higher education levels for women, while **death rates** continue to level off.
 
 
 
• **Stage 4: Low Stationary**
 
 
• Characterized by **low birth rates** and **low death rates**, reflecting a high level of economic development and modern lifestyle, leading to zero or very low population growth.
 
 
 
• **Factors Driving Mortality Decline**
 
 
• Key historical drivers include the **Green Revolution** which boosted crop yields and the discovery of **antibiotics** and **antiseptics** which drastically reduced infectious disease fatalities.

questions.question: In the reaction Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(*) + 2NaCl(aq), what will be the actual physical state that can replace (*)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**(s)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The reaction provided, **Na₂SO₄(aq) + BaCl₂(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2NaCl(aq)**, is a classic example of a **double displacement reaction**.
 
• In this chemical process, the **sodium (Na⁺)** and **barium (Ba²⁺)** ions exchange their partners (**sulfate** and **chloride** ions) to form two new compounds.
 
• When aqueous solutions of **sodium sulfate** and **barium chloride** are mixed, a chemical change occurs that results in the formation of **barium sulfate** and **sodium chloride**.
 
• **Barium sulfate (BaSO₄)** is highly **insoluble** in water. As soon as it is formed, it settles out of the solution as a **white precipitate**.
 
• In chemical notation, the physical state of a **precipitate** (a solid that forms from a liquid solution) is denoted by the symbol **(s)**, which stands for **solid**.
 
• The other product, **sodium chloride (NaCl)**, remains in the **aqueous** state (dissolved in water), which is why it is marked as **(aq)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Precipitation Reactions**:

 
 
• These occur when two **soluble ionic salts** are mixed in an aqueous solution to produce an **insoluble ionic compound**.
 
• The **solubility rules** dictate that most **sulfates** are soluble, but **barium sulfate** is a notable exception, making it a common precipitate in analytical chemistry.
 
 
 
• **Understanding State Symbols**:
 
 
• **(s) - Solid**: Used for reactants or products that are in the **solid phase**, including precipitates.
 
• **(l) - Liquid**: Used for pure substances in a **liquid state**, such as **H₂O** or molten metals.
 
• **(g) - Gas**: Used for substances that exist in the **gaseous state** at the reaction conditions, like **CO₂** or **H₂**.
 
• **(aq) - Aqueous**: Derived from the Latin word **aqua**, it indicates that the substance is **dissolved in water** as a solvent.
 
 
 
• **Double Displacement Characteristics**:
 
 
• These reactions often result in the formation of a **precipitate**, a **gas**, or a **neutral molecular compound** like water (in neutralization reactions).

• Following the death of **Raja Ram Mohan Roy** in **1833** in **Bristol**, the movement went through a period of decline and lacked a formal leadership structure for nearly a decade.

• He merged the **Tattvabodhini Sabha** with the **Brahmo Samaj** and introduced the **Brahmo Covenant**, a set of solemn vows to ensure a disciplined religious life for its members.

questions.question: A user is leaving their laptop unattended for the entire weekend and wants to ensure zero battery consumption while still being able to resume their exact work session (all open applications and files) quickly when they return on Monday. Which power-saving mode in Windows should they choose?

options.text: Hybrid Sleep, because it uses both RAM and the hard drive to store the session.
Hibernate, because it saves the entire system state to the hard disk and powers down completely.
Shut Down, because it is the only way to achieve zero power consumption.
Sleep (Standby), because it maintains the session in RAM for a very quick resume.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hibernate, because it saves the entire system state to the hard disk and powers down completely.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hibernate** mode is specifically designed for laptops and mobile devices to preserve the **operating state** without consuming any **electrical power** from the battery.
 
• When a computer enters this state, it takes all the information currently stored in the **Random Access Memory (RAM)** and writes it into a hidden system file on the **Hard Disk Drive (HDD)** or **Solid State Drive (SSD)** known as **hiberfil.sys**.
 
• Since the data is stored on **non-volatile storage** (the disk) rather than **volatile memory** (RAM), the system can safely **power down completely**, achieving **zero battery consumption** over long periods like a **weekend**.
 
• Upon restarting the device, the **Windows Boot Manager** retrieves the saved state from the disk and loads it back into **RAM**, allowing the user to resume their **exact work session** with all **open applications** and files intact.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Power Management Modes**:

 
 
• **Sleep (Standby)**: Keeps the session in **RAM** and uses a small amount of **power**. It allows for an almost **instant resume**, but if the **battery dies**, any unsaved work is lost.
 
• **Hybrid Sleep**: Primarily used for **Desktop PCs**, it saves the session to both **RAM** and the **hard disk**. It uses power to keep the **RAM** active but provides a backup on the disk in case of a **power failure**.
 
• **Shut Down**: Completely closes all **software programs**, clears the **RAM**, and turns off the hardware. It does not save the **user session** or open files.
 
• **Fast Startup**: A feature in **Windows 10 and 11** that combines **Hibernate** and **Shut Down** to decrease boot time by saving the **OS kernel** state to the disk while closing **user applications**.

questions.question: Electrical conductors are materials that possess which of the following properties?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Low resistivity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Electrical conductors** are substances that facilitate the easy movement of **electric charges** (primarily electrons) through them when an external **electric field** is applied.
 
• The fundamental property that defines a good conductor is **low resistivity** (represented by the Greek letter **ρ**), which implies that the material offers minimal opposition to the flow of **electric current**.
 
• Resistivity is the intrinsic property of a material that quantifies how strongly it resists electric current; for conductors like **Silver**, **Copper**, and **Aluminum**, this value is extremely small, typically ranging from **10−⁸ Ω⋅m** to **10−⁶ Ω⋅m**.
 
• According to **Ohm's Law**, the resistance of a conductor is directly proportional to its resistivity; therefore, a material with **low resistivity** will have **low resistance**, allowing a higher current to flow for a given **potential difference**.
 
• The **electrical conductivity** (σ) is the reciprocal of resistivity (σ = 1/ρ); hence, conductors characterized by **low resistivity** possess **high electrical conductivity**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **High resistivity**:

 
 
• This is a characteristic feature of **insulators** such as **glass**, **rubber**, and **ebonite**.
 
• These materials have very few **free electrons**, preventing the flow of charge and resulting in resistivity values often exceeding **10¹² Ω⋅m**.
 
 
 
• **No resistivity**:
 
 
• This state is achieved by **superconductors** when they are cooled below a specific **critical temperature**.
 
• In this state, the material exhibits **zero electrical resistance** and expels **magnetic fields** (the **Meissner effect**).
 
 
 
• **Factors affecting Resistivity**:
 
 
• Resistivity is not constant for all conditions; it depends on the **nature of the material** and its **temperature**.
 
• For metallic conductors, resistivity typically increases with an **increase in temperature** due to increased collisions between electrons and **lattice ions**.

questions.question: Which first-of-its-kind propellant-production device did ISRO unveil in February 2025?

• **Vertical Planetary Mixer Technology**:

questions.question: Which river rises west of the Rohtang pass in the Kullu hills of Himachal Pradesh and flows through the Chamba valley of the state?

• Geographically, the river drains the area situated between the **Pir Panjal** range to the north and the **Dhauladhar** range to the south.

questions.question: A student notices that arithmetic results appear instantly, but loading data from main memory is slower. Which CPU feature primarily reduces this delay by keeping frequently used data close to the processor?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cache Memory**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cache Memory** is a high-speed, volatile **SRAM (Static Random Access Memory)** buffer located directly on or very close to the **Central Processing Unit (CPU)** chip to facilitate rapid data retrieval.
 
• Its primary objective is to bridge the speed gap between the high-speed **Processor** and the relatively slower **Main Memory (DRAM)** by storing copies of the most frequently used data and instructions.
 
• When the **CPU** requires data, it initiates a **Cache Look-up**; if the data is present (a **Cache Hit**), it is processed nearly instantly, whereas a **Cache Miss** forces the system to fetch data from **RAM**, which takes significantly more clock cycles.
 
• Modern systems utilize a **Memory Hierarchy** consisting of **L1** (fastest, smallest, per core), **L2** (intermediate speed/size), and **L3** (largest, shared across cores) caches to optimize **Instruction Throughput** and reduce **Latency**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Address Decoder**:

 
 
• It is a combinational logic circuit that identifies specific **Memory Locations** or **Registers** based on the binary address provided by the **CPU**.
 
• While it is crucial for routing data during **Read/Write Operations**, it does not function as a storage medium or a speed-enhancing buffer.
 
 
 
• **Instruction Set**:
 
 
• Also known as **Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)**, it represents the collection of basic commands (like **MOV**, **ADD**, or **HLT**) that a processor is designed to understand.
 
• Common architectures include **x86** (CISC) and **ARM** (RISC), defining how software communicates with the hardware.
 
 
 
• **CPU Fan**:
 
 
• An active cooling component that prevents **Thermal Throttling** by dissipating heat generated by the **Transistors**.
 
• It ensures the **Processor** remains within safe **Operating Temperatures** but does not interact with the data-loading logic or memory cycles.

questions.question: Which seismic waves are the fastest and travel through both solids and liquids inside the Earth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**P waves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **P waves**, also known as **Primary waves**, are the fastest of all seismic waves and are the first to be recorded by a **seismograph** after an earthquake occurs.
 
• These waves are **longitudinal** or **compressional** in nature, meaning the particles of the medium vibrate in the same direction as the wave propagation, creating a **push-pull** effect.
 
• A defining characteristic of **P waves** is their ability to travel through all states of matter, including **solids**, **liquids**, and **gases**; this allows them to pass through the **Earth's mantle** as well as the **liquid outer core**.
 
• The velocity of these waves depends on the **compressibility** and **density** of the material they pass through, typically traveling at speeds between **1.5 to 8 kilometers per second** in the Earth's crust.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **S waves**:

 
 
• Also called **Secondary waves** or **shear waves**, these are slower than P waves and arrive second at seismic stations.
 
• They move particles up and down or side-to-side, perpendicular to the direction of wave travel, and can only propagate through **solid materials**.
 
• Their inability to travel through the **liquid outer core** provided the first scientific evidence that the Earth has a liquid layer.
 
 
 
• **Surface waves**:
 
 
• These waves travel strictly along the **Earth's surface** rather than through its deep interior and are responsible for the most severe **structural damage** during an earthquake.
 
• **Rayleigh waves** are a type of surface wave that moves the ground in an **elliptical motion**, similar to ocean waves.
 
• **Love waves** are another type of surface wave that causes horizontal shifting of the Earth's crust.
